en: The *Dharmādarśa Sūtra*, translated by An Xuan, Cavalry Commandant from the kingdom of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the country of Mṛgadhara at the Śirīṣa tree grove.

At the Ghoṣitārāma, he was together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty *bhikṣus* who had removed their impurities, as well as five hundred bodhisattvas, including Maitreya, Gītamati, Prajñākūṭa, and Akṣayamati, who were the foremost among the bodhisattvas.
At that time, several hundred people surrounded and crowded around the Blessed One as he preached the sutra.

Then, from the city of Śrāvastī, a householder named Jeta, accompanied by five hundred followers, emerged from the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Arriving at the place where the Blessed One was, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and sat down on a seat.

Furthermore, there were those of the school of logic named Zaiyu (Loving Encounter), Naiyu (Indeed Encounter), Shanshou (Good Bestowal), Dawei (Great Majesty), Jiguduju (Cluster of the Lonely and Poor), Longwei (Dragon Majesty), and Disi (True Contemplation). All these five hundred members of the assembly together proceeded to the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, they bowed their heads at the feet of the World-Honored One and all took their seats before him.

All those householders have set their minds upon seeking the Great Way; together with their followers, they have all cultivated the roots of virtue and resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, with the sole exception of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Thereupon, the householder Śrigupta, seeing that the great assembly of householders had gathered and were seated, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated himself, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed them, saying:
"I wish to ask a question. Would the Blessed One have the leisure to expound upon what I ask?"
The World-Honored One replied to the householder Śreṇika:

"The Tathāgata always has the leisure to expound upon what you ask, householder. Ask whatever you wish; seek from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, whatever you desire. I shall expound upon your questions for your sake, so as to fulfill your intent."
The householder Śreṇika asked the Buddha:
"In this regard, O Blessed One! If a son or daughter of good family resolves to seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path;

delights in the Great Way, practices the Great Way, desires to attain the Great Way, desires to descend into the Great Way, and desires to know the Great Way; and if they invite all sentient beings, comfort sentient beings, and rescue and protect sentient beings, making this vow:"
"Those who have not yet crossed over, I shall cause them to cross;
those who have not yet been liberated, I shall cause them to be liberated;
those who are not at peace, I shall bring them to peace."
"Those who have not yet attained parinirvāṇa, I shall lead them to parinirvāṇa.

For the sake of undertaking the heavy responsibility for all sentient beings and desiring to rescue and protect them, he made this vow, swearing this great and vast oath. Aware of the manifold evils within birth and death, his mind was never weary; through countless kalpas of birth and death, his resolve never slackened.
"Furthermore, O Venerable One!
There may be bodhisattvas who leave home to practice the Way and thereby attain the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment, or there may be those who remain at home.
Excellent, O Venerable One!"

Out of compassion for sentient beings, and to bestow grace upon those who follow this Great Way so that the Three Jewels may flourish, and furthermore so that all who are diligent in the scriptures may cause them to endure for a long time, the Tathāgata should please explain the methods for the training and virtue of lay bodhisattvas.
What is meant by this, O World-Honored One?
It is that a bodhisattva living at home who receives and follows the Tathāgata’s instructions does not diminish nor impair their original vow— namely, the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path—
and furthermore manifests faultless conduct in the present life and proceeds toward the most excellent path in future lives.
Furthermore, O Honored One among the Multitudes!

When a bodhisattva leaves the household life to pursue the Way, they renounce hatred and attachment, shave off their beard and hair, and don the dharma robes. Having left the household while possessing faith, they leave home to practice the Way, manifesting therein the full display of instruction, formal rules, correct standards, and virtuous models.
“O Householder! For a bodhisattva who has left the household life to practice the Way, as well as for one who remains at home, how should they cultivate it?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the householder with these words of profound principle:
“Excellent, excellent, householder!
It is well that you now know to ask the Tathāgata about the practices performed by bodhisattvas, both those living at home and those who have gone forth from home.
Therefore, householder!”
"Listen now to what I shall say; exert yourselves to reflect upon it well. This is the practice of virtuous conduct for a bodhisattva living at home who pursues the Way.
The householder listened with great earnestness as he received the instruction.
The World-Honored One said: "In this regard, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home who practices the Way should take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha."
By virtue of the root of merit from that taking of refuge, it is transformed into unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Householder!
What is meant by taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?

I shall adorn myself by accomplishing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man that constitute the Buddha-body; furthermore, I shall bring forth those thirty-two marks of a Great Man through the roots of virtue, and having attained those roots of virtue, I shall practice them with diligent effort.
That a bodhisattva living at home takes refuge in the Buddha is as described above.
What is meant by taking refuge in the Dharma?

It means to revere the Dharma, to seek the Dharma, to desire the Dharma, to delight in the joy of the Dharma, to exalt the Dharma, to rely upon the Dharma, to protect the Dharma, and to be cautious regarding the Dharma; to abide according to the Dharma, to follow the methods of the Dharma, to serve as a repository for the Dharma, to possess the power of the Dharma, to seek the wealth of the Dharma, to cultivate the tranquility of the Dharma, and to perform deeds of the Dharma, thinking: "I, too, shall distribute this Dharma throughout the heavens and the world."
For a lay bodhisattva, taking refuge in the Dharma is as follows.
What is meant by taking refuge in the Saṃgha?

If a lay bodhisattva sees one who has attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), arhat (arhat), or even an ordinary person seeking the path of a disciple, they shall show them respect, serve and provide for them, honor and revere them, and treat them with propriety.
If one attains this aspiration by serving that True Dharma and its correct methods, then I too shall attain the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path.
By expounding the sutras and bringing about the virtue of disciples, one honors them; how could one not admire them?
When a bodhisattva living as a householder takes refuge in the Saṅgha, it is for this reason.
Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva takes refuge in the Buddha by cultivating four dharmas.
What are the four?

First, the aspiration for the Way is never abandoned until the end; second, that which has been received is never transgressed until the end; third, great compassion is never severed until the end; fourth, heterodox paths are never pursued until the end.
These are the four dharmas.
For a lay bodhisattva who takes refuge in the Buddha, it is as follows.
Furthermore, householder, by practicing four dharmas, one takes refuge in the Dharma.
What are the four?
First, one serves and follows those who speak on all dharmas;
second, one treats the Dharma one has heard with reverence.
Third, having heard the Dharma, one contemplates its beginning and end;
fourth, according to the Dharma as it has been heard, one explains it in detail for others according to their capacity.
These are the four dharmas.
It is in this manner that a lay bodhisattva takes refuge in the Dharma.
"Furthermore, householder!
One cultivates four dharmas to take refuge in the Saṃgha.
What are the four?
First, one should aspire to give rise to the path of a disciple, while maintaining a mind that delights in all forms of wisdom.
Second, he also treats accumulated things as accumulations of Dharma and transforms them through that accumulation;
third, he relies upon a community that possesses dependence and resolution, rather than relying upon a community of disciples;
fourth, he seeks the virtues of his disciples and does not deliver them by means of measuring their virtues.
These are the four dharmas.
It is in this manner that a bodhisattva living at home takes refuge in the Saṃgha.
"Furthermore, householder!
Practicing the Way while living at home, one contemplates the Buddha upon seeing the Tathāgata; this is taking refuge in the Buddha.
Having heard the Dharma, one contemplates the Dharma; this is taking refuge in the Dharma.
If, having seen the noble assembly of the Tathāgata, one still contemplates the intention of the Path, this is taking refuge in the Saṃgha.
"Furthermore, householder!
When practicing the Way while living at home, if one gives with the aspiration to encounter a Buddha, this constitutes taking refuge in the Buddha;
if one gives for the sake of upholding the True Dharma, this constitutes taking refuge in the Dharma."
"If one has already practiced giving for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, they take refuge in the Sangha.
Furthermore, householder, you who practice the Way while living at home!"
If one cultivates the conduct of a noble person and does not act with the conduct of an ordinary person, that is the conduct of a noble person.
Seeking wealth through the Dharma and not through what is contrary to the Dharma, doing so with integrity and not with depravity—this likewise constitutes right livelihood.
One does not coerce others through harassment, but brings them to compliance through the Dharma.
When wealth is abundant, one cultivates the perception of impermanence and accepts treasures accordingly; thus, one remains perpetually prosperous.

One bestows gifts and makes offerings to parents, teachers, friends, subordinates, brothers, and relatives as an act of reverence; likewise, one ensures that slaves, guests, and attendants are treated with impartial care, thereby providing them with instruction and transformation.
This sublime Dharma also involves undertaking a heavy responsibility; this is called the heavy responsibility of sentient beings.
To practice with diligence and without slackening, yet not to accept that heavy responsibility—by not accepting it—one says that these disciples each engage in the affairs of Buddha-wisdom.
He brings sentient beings to maturity without weariness, not craving personal pleasure but seeking to bring about the happiness of sentient beings.
He is unmoved by gain or loss, defamation or praise, honor or ridicule, suffering or joy; he transcends worldly dharmas and does not feel elated even when possessing great wealth.
Furthermore, within the three realms, he experiences neither profit nor renown, no fame, and no reward.
One’s actions are preceded by careful reflection; one takes joy in receiving what is correct. Having understood the essentials through right perception and insight, one maintains right conduct.
Having already resolved the duality of praise and blame, one attains what was vowed and attends to human affairs with earnestness, never neglecting one's duties.

When one has bestowed kindness upon others, one never expects a reward in return; having performed acts of charity to a certain extent, one recognizes that kindness and its reciprocity, thereby cultivating the practice of virtuous merit.

He bestows wealth upon the poor; he brings peace and security to those who are afraid; he relieves the grief of those who are sorrowful; he exercises patience toward those who are weak; and he diminishes the arrogance of the powerful, thereby abandoning all forms of excessive pride and extreme conceit.
By showing reverence to elders, serving those of great learning, and being able to question those of clear knowledge;
by manifesting straightforwardness without artifice toward the multitude, and practicing with skillful means—one’s virtue may indeed be sought!
To be insatiable and tireless in extensive learning, to practice correctly with diligent effort, and to firmly encounter the sages;
to follow the sages and revere them, to serve those who have heard much and to question those who possess knowledge—this is how one manifests straightforwardness.
Without relying on secret scriptures, he manifests for others what he has heard and clarifies the meaning of what he has heard:

"All the pleasures and delights of desire are reckoned as impermanent; one does not cherish or begrudge the body, observing one's own life as a drop of morning dew, and regarding all possessions and wealth as illusory clouds."

One regards one's family and guests as enemies; one regards one's wife, children, and grandchildren as the Avīci Hell; one regards all that one possesses as every form of suffering; and one constantly regards fields, houses, dwellings, and all things upon which one exerts effort as defects.
One should regard the virtues one seeks to achieve as being subject to decay;
one’s household life as being perilous;
and one’s friends, ministers, brothers, and relatives as being the wardens of hell.
Throughout the day and night, they maintain a single perception:
regarding this unreal body, they perceive it as real;
regarding this unreal lifespan, they perceive it as real.
With unreal wealth, one forms the perception that it is real.
If such a person uses ritual propriety to manage various affairs and serves others with respect, they are thereby using an unreal body as if it were real.
If one does not destroy the foundation of past manifold virtues and further increases their excellence, it is by means of this unreal life that one receives the real.
Likewise, if one restrains stinginess and distributes bounty and bestows virtue, it is by means of this unreal wealth that one receives the real.
This is the conduct of a worthy man for a bodhisattva practicing the Way while living at home; acting in this manner, he incurs no fault.
It is to speak the words of the Tathāgata and to speak the Dharma;
neither does he disparage nor does he damage his original vow—this is called the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way.
Thus, one will have conduct free from transgression in the present life and shall also fall upon the most excellent path in future lives.
"Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva dwelling at home who cultivates the Way should personally uphold the matter of the precepts; that is to say, the matter of upholding the five precepts."
For this reason, he does not take pleasure in killing living beings; he does not apply blades or sticks to even the smallest crawling creatures, nor does he harass or constrain others.

For this reason, he does not take pleasure in stealing the property of others; he is content with what he possesses himself and does not set his mind upon the wealth of others. As for even the slightest things, such as blades of grass or stalks of grain, if they are not given, he will never take them.
For this reason, he does not take pleasure in the depravity of lust; he is content with his own wife and does not even look with desire at the women of others.
The mind should always regard itself as afflicted, reflecting that desire is entirely suffering.

If one should give rise to a lustful thought toward one's own wife, one should contemplate her as a foul impurity and maintain a sense of dread. Toiling for the sake of desire is done without fear or the realization of suffering; yet because of longing for what is impermanent, one harbors notions of purity and pleasure. It is with such an understanding that I shall cultivate myself.
If one does not even entertain such desires through thought, how much less would they arise repeatedly?
Therefore, one should not delight in false speech, but should speak with truth and sincerity;
one should possess a nature free from deceit and fraud.
With an unyielding mind and sincere integrity, one speaks exactly as one has seen and heard;
one carefully guards the sutras and the Dharma, not sparing even one's own body or life, and thus refrains from false speech.

Therefore, one should not be fond of drinking alcohol; by not becoming intoxicated, one avoids confusion and agitation, remains free from punishment, accords with transformation, strengthens the will, and maintains correct knowledge.

"If one were to restore the intention for giving, I would give everything to others: seeking food, I would give food; seeking drink, I would give drink; seeking a vehicle, I would give a vehicle; seeking clothing, I would give clothing. Thus, by giving wine to establish their resolve, such is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)."
At that time, if there was anyone who asked for anything, I would give it to them.
At that time, I was able to offer wine so as to transform their wills; thus, acting according to my own understanding, I remained free from delusion.
Why is this so? It is because a bodhisattva fulfills the aspirations of sentient beings; such is the perfection of giving, and it is thus in every respect.
When a bodhisattva living at home gives wine to others, he incurs no offense.
Therefore, O Householder!

A bodhisattva transforms the roots of virtue cultivated through his training into the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path; if he practices well, he should carefully observe and protect these five precepts.

Furthermore, one who possesses excellence should not slander others; when there is strife, they should bring about harmony. They should avoid coarse speech and instead always speak first with gentle words. They should not engage in frivolous talk, but rather speak for the sake of meaning, for the sake of the Dharma, at the proper time, and in accordance with reality.
They should be free from the net of delusion and bestow peace and security upon all sentient beings.
Their mind shall not be corrupt or disordered, but shall always be adorned by the power of patience.

"By means of right view, one abandons and distances oneself from wrong views; this is why one bows one's head to the Buddhas and the assembly of those who have received blessings, and not to other heavenly deities.
Furthermore, householder!

For those who practice the Way while living at home—whether in villages, hamlets, districts, counties, states, or cities—they should protect and uphold the sutras and the Dharma there. How, then, does one protect and uphold the sutras?
Those who lack faith are transformed through the teaching of faith;
those who are stingy and greedy are transformed through the teaching of generosity;
those with evil precepts are transformed through the teaching of the precepts.
Those with distracted minds are taught and transformed through patience;
those who are indolent are taught and transformed through diligence;
and those who have lost their resolve are taught and transformed through contemplation.
Those with false knowledge he transforms through the application of wisdom;
those impoverished of wealth he enriches;
and those who are ill he provides with medicine.
They shall serve as family for the solitary,
as a refuge for those without refuge,
and as a reliance for those without reliance; for all those who dwell in kingdoms and towns, they shall protect the sutras and the Dharma in this manner.
“Householder!
Perhaps that bodhisattva, having gone once, twice, three times, or even up to a hundred times, instructs and exhorts the people, causing them all to cultivate the dharmas of manifold virtues.”
That bodhisattva then applies compassion to sentient beings and strengthens them all with solemn vows.
His vow is expressed in these words:
"As long as these people who are difficult to transform have not attained accomplishment, I shall never take up the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path."
Why is this so? It is because, for this very reason, I have made a vow to myself: "I shall not [be one who] is merely straightforward;

I shall not [be one who] is merely not sycophantic; I shall not [be one who] is merely not deceitful; I shall not [be one who] is merely observant; I shall not [be one who] is merely admonishing the virtuous."
For the sake of these people, I have made this vow to myself; it is solely because I wish to cause these people to hear the Dharma of the sutras, so that they may transform me through the sutras.
For this reason, I have made this vow to myself.
I shall constantly strengthen my diligent practice; thus, my skillful means will not be in vain.
Should anyone behold me, there shall be none who does not respond with wholesome faith.
If a householder reaches the dwelling of a bodhisattva and fails to cease their lamentation, such that all the people fall into various evil realms, that is the fault of the bodhisattva.
"Householder!

It is like this: suppose there were a skilled physician in a village, town, district, province, or kingdom, down to the smallest settlement; if even a single person among them did not die before their natural lifespan, everyone would blame that physician."
In this way, householder!

If a bodhisattva, while residing in his dwelling, does not refrain from lamenting that all people fall into various evil paths, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would hold that bodhisattva at fault.
"Householder! For this reason, a householder bodhisattva makes this vow to himself:
'Even if I should go to a kingdom or town where the people are base and foolish, I shall not allow even a single person to fall into the evil realms.'"
"Furthermore, householder!
One who practices the Way while living at home should understand the evils of the household life.
To dwell in a household is to bring harm to the root of all that is wholesome; because the household offers no means of escape and harms the Dharma of purity, it is called 'home' (gṛha)."

To dwell at home means to dwell amidst all manner of toil, to dwell with thoughts of manifold evils, and to dwell with manifold evil deeds; it is to be untransformed and lacking self-restraint, to dwell together with foolish commoners, and to assemble with those who lack discernment—therefore, it is called "home."
A "home" (kula) is merely a name; yet once one is situated within it, there is nothing one will not do that is contrary to the Way.

Because of being situated therein, one fails to show reverence toward one's parents, those whose minds are stilled, those whose minds have passed beyond, elders, and the various noble ones; for this reason, it is called a "home."

The county officials' prisons, with their interrogations, floggings, beatings, and verbal abuse, leading ultimately to death—all these arise from that [the family]; therefore, it is called the "family."
To be therein is to enter the evil realms; to be therein is to fall into various desires, to fall into hatred, to dwell amidst all fears, and to dwell in ignorance—this is what is called "home."

Because one does not carefully guard those matters of precept, because one distances oneself from the matter of concentration, because one does not cultivate the matter of wisdom, because one does not attain deliverance, and because one does not give rise to the knowledge and vision of deliverance—for these reasons, it is called "home."

Because these exist therein—namely, love for one's parents, love for brothers and sisters, love for one's wife and children, love for one's house and property, love for servants and guests, love for all possessions, and the insatiable craving for wealth—it is therefore called "home."
How difficult it is for those living as householders to be satisfied!
They are like the great ocean, into which all streams flow.
How they never know satiety!
It is like fire obtaining fuel;
those who dwell in the household have many thoughts and find no rest.
It is like wind that has no place to settle; they are still submerged in the depths.
If delicious food and drink are mixed with poison, all that exists is suffering!
It is like an enemy appearing in the guise of a friend; it leads people astray in their conduct!
It is not what the scriptures prescribe; it creates discord and strife!
Constantly entangled with one another, they remain in perpetual disharmony.
How full of blemishes they are!
Because one performs deeds of good and evil, wherever the conditions for those deeds lie, one is constantly suspected by others.
It is not that such people do not exist;
it is because they possess inverted views.
How truly unwholesome!
Though there may be skillful means and artifice within what appears wholesome, one still perceives their underlying nature and conduct;
it is like the very essence of a courtesan!
Because they change so rapidly,
they are like a magician!
Those who have newly arrived gather in crowds, and their conduct is insincere.
It is like a dream!
For all things arise and perish, having a beginning and an end.
It is like the morning dew!
Because it is quickly departed from,
it is like a drop of honey;
because its flavor is slight.
It is like a net of *śṛṅgāṭaka* thorns,
for one is harmed by forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
It is like a "needle-holed" insect!
Because they take unwholesome thoughts as their sustenance,
they are like those who disobey commands;
for they act by deceiving one another.
One is constantly filled with fear!
This is because the mind is in a state of disorder.
Is this not due to being overly social?
This is because officials, bandits, enemies, and wicked kings cause harm.
For those living at home, there is little flavor or joy;
they consider this to be the loss resulting from much evil.
"Householder!
A bodhisattva living at home should understand the evils of the household to be such as these.
Furthermore, householder!"
For those who practice the Way while living at home, giving is their treasure. That which has already been given is what belongs to them; that which remains at home does not belong to them.
That which has already been given is a treasure; that which remains at home is not a treasure.
That which has already been given constitutes wealth; that which remains at home constitutes a lack of wealth.
If one has already practiced giving, it results in the alleviation of toil; whereas for those living at home, toil increases.
If one has already practiced giving, it results in non-self; whereas for those living at home, there is the sense of self.
If one has already practiced giving, it results in non-existence; whereas for those living at home, they regard things as existent.
If one regards giving as inexhaustible, yet regards living at home as impermanent;
if, having given, one no longer guards [the gift], yet regards living at home as guarding it;
if one regards giving as the conduct of a noble man, yet regards living at home as the mind of an ordinary person;
If one has already practiced giving, they rely on the path of the transcendent perfections; if one remains a householder, they rely on heterodox factions.
If one has already practiced giving, they are praised by the Buddhas; if one remains a householder, they are praised by fools.
Householder!
For a bodhisattva dwelling at home who cultivates the Way, giving is a treasure such as this.
Therefore, when they see someone come seeking something, they give rise to three thoughts.
What are the three?

The perception of a virtuous friend, the perception of relying on the path of the perfections, and the perception of striving to produce abundant wealth—these are the three perceptions for which one should strive.
Furthermore, one should cultivate another three perceptions.
What are the three?
They are the perception of the Tathāgata’s instructions as supreme, the subduing of perverse perceptions, and the perception of not seeking merit. Why is this so?
If this bodhisattva encounters those who come seeking anything, their greed, anger, and delusion will become attenuated; as for how these are attenuated, what is it like?
If one gives away all possessions without any sense of惜惜 (reluctance or attachment), this is the attenuation of greed and lust;
if one treats those who come to seek things with compassion and pity, this is the attenuation of anger and hatred;
if one transforms all these through giving and becomes skillful in this regard, this is called the attenuation of ignorance.
"Furthermore, householder!
Having seen those who come seeking material goods, one shall before long fulfill the practice of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
How does one fulfill them? [As follows:]"
If there is someone who comes and asks for things from another, and that person is able to give without being stingy, this is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā);
if one gives while keeping the mind fixed on the Path, this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā);
if one does not become angry or resentful, this is the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Even if one should still harbor such thoughts, what use is there for food?
To strengthen one's resolve and not abandon one's practice—this is the *pāramitā* of vigor (*vīrya*).
Whether one intends to give or has already given, to be free from distress and without regret—this is the *pāramitā* of reflection (*cintā*).
If one has already given and does not look for its merit, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Householder!
It is in this way that a bodhisattva accomplishes the practice of the six perfections through giving.
"Furthermore, householder!
One who dwells at home must distance themselves from following after anger and agitation, for this is the nature of separation from those one holds dear.
Even if they acquire property, wealth, grain, or children, they do not regard these as a cause for joy."
If all things perish and come to ruin, one does not become sorrowful or distressed by such thoughts;
having contemplated all phenomena as being like an illusion, one does not dwell upon the notion of permanence.

Such is the practice of illusion that leads to this state: therefore, parents, wife, children, slaves, and guests are not mine to possess; I am not their possessor; I do not exist as such; I ought not to exist as such; for it is because I am not that they exist.
"Now, for his sake, I have committed evil deeds; this existence belongs only to the present life and not to the future life.
This was my past existence, and it is not something I must protect."
Furthermore, regarding that which belongs to the self, we ought to protect it.
What is meant by "that which belongs to the self"?
It refers to the practice of giving and transformation, the tranquil and self-restrained root of the Way, and the hidden foundation of virtue; this is what constitutes that which belongs to the self.
As for those who follow me wherever I dwell, they likewise do not commit evil deeds for the sake of their bodies or lives, nor for the sake of their sons, daughters, wives, or households.
Therefore, those who live as householders and have wives should cultivate three perceptions.
What are these three?
The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-duration, and the perception of separation—these three perceptions should be cultivated.
Furthermore, one should cultivate three perceptions. What are these three?

If one is in joy and pleasure, it is for the sake of seeking future suffering; if one is in food and drink, it is for the sake of seeking calamity and transgression; if one is in happiness, it is for the sake of seeking suffering. One should cultivate these three perceptions.
Furthermore, one should cultivate three perceptions.
What are the three?
The perception of accumulation, the perception of depletion, and the perception of what belongs to the mundane; these three perceptions should be cultivated.
Furthermore, one should cultivate three perceptions.
What are the three?
They are the perception of entering hell, the perception of entering the animal realm, and the perception of entering the realm of spirits and ghosts; these three perceptions should be cultivated.
Furthermore, one should cultivate three perceptions.
What are the three?
They are the perception of goblins and specters, the perception of pestilence, and the perception of physical forms; these are the three perceptions to be cultivated.
Furthermore, one should cultivate three perceptions.
What are the three?
The perception of non-self, the perception of ownerlessness, and the perception of being like a borrowed object; these three perceptions should be cultivated.
Householder!
When you contemplate these various thoughts regarding a bodhisattva living at home, you should observe yourself and your wife in this same way.
Therefore, you should not cherish your children; even if you have no affection for your own offspring, let it not exceed that which you feel for all people in the world.
Therefore, one should admonish oneself by means of three counts, admonishing one's own mind.
What are these three?
To have an even mind is the Way; it is not to have a deviant mind.
Right practice constitutes the Way; it is not through wrong practice.
Fewer actions constitute the Way; many actions are contrary to it.
Therefore, one should admonish oneself three times, repeatedly admonishing one's own mind, and conceive toward one's children the notion of an enemy, thinking: "This is my enemy, not my friend."
Why is this? Because I have violated the compassionate instructions of the Buddha, I have caused my craving for them to increase excessively.
One must discipline one's own mind, as if one’s love were directed toward an only son, and extend that same love to all sentient beings.
If one loves oneself, one should extend compassion and pity toward all sentient beings.
Therefore, one should contemplate the beginning and end of this matter: that which has come from here is distinct, and that from which I have come is likewise distinct.
Sentient beings were once my children in previous lives, and I too was once a child of sentient beings; this is the fault of birth and death, wherein there is no distinction between kin and stranger.
Why is this so? On whatever path one travels, there will inevitably arise those who act with detachment, and they will in turn become enemies.
Therefore, I shall now cultivate myself such that I have no friends at all, nor do I have any enemies.
Why is this so? Because one who forms acquaintances does so with the desire to act much; because one who forms enmities does so entirely out of a desire for evil.
All sentient beings are not the self; your mind should not be governed by the notions of "acceptable" or "unacceptable," for you must master all the scriptures. Why is this so?
Those who practice correctly attain the right path; those who practice erroneously attain the wrong path.
Now, I am free from erroneous conduct and possess correct mental application toward all sentient beings; thus, I shall attain all forms of agility.
“Householder!

For a bodhisattva living at home, there is nothing whatsoever to be longed for, nothing to be admired, nothing to be attached to, nothing to be cherished, and nothing to be desired; it is in this manner that he acts.
Furthermore, householder!
Suppose a person comes to a householder with a request, and even if he does not wish to give that person the object, he should still admonish himself and reflect on his intention:
"If I do not give this object as a gift, I will inevitably be separated from it."
Whether one desires it or not, at the time of death, these things must also be abandoned by me, and I too must abandon them.
If one gives away treasures before the end, and I give away these things, then at the time of death, the mind will be free from attachment.
Even if one reflects in this manner, if one is unable to give that object away, one should decline those who come seeking the object with four kinds of excuses.
What are these four?
I am without power, my manifold virtues are not yet perfected;
I am at the very beginning of the Great Path, and my intention to practice giving is not yet free.
I possess views regarding what is received, and these reside within my remaining conduct; therefore, please grant me your forgiveness, O Worthy One, and do not press me too hard.
If one can practice what I have taught and carry it out exactly as received, only then will one be able to fulfill the wishes of you and all people in the world.
Such is the manner in which one should decline those who come to solicit goods.
"Furthermore, householder!

For one who practices the Way while living at home, even if they are separated from the instructions of a teacher, and there is no Buddha in the world, no one who has seen the scriptures, and no encounter with the noble Saṅgha, they should nevertheless prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions. They should also reflect upon the vast aspirations and the practices undertaken in previous lives by those seeking the Way, and pray that all such virtues for accomplishing the Buddha-dharma may be fulfilled, rejoicing in them through such contemplation."
Thereupon, three times during the day and three times at night, he discussed the matters of the three categories of sūtras.
He confessed all the evils he had committed in previous lives, reforming his past ways and cultivating himself for the future, seeking compassion from all Buddhas;
out of regard for the Dharma, they took pity on him, and they also took pity on him through the infinite and boundless Dharmas.
“Furthermore, householder!

One who dwells at home while practicing the Way should understand the ritual for calming the mind. Therefore, if you see one who has removed the afflictions, who is transcendent, and who observes the ritual for calming the mind, you should revere their Dharma robe; for it is the Dharma garment worn by those who are the Benefactors of the Multitude, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and those who practice the precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the Buddha.”
By being free from evil, one abandons all evils; such a person is the exemplar of the many noble ṛṣis.
Therefore, one should revere them and likewise show compassion toward those who are still seeking nourishment (pudgala); it is not for the wise to engage in such unprincipled conduct.
"As for their attire, those known as 'the tranquil,' 'the disciplined,' 'the supernaturally empowered,' and 'the Tathāgatas' manifest it as a practice that is undisciplined and impure."
Furthermore, the Tathāgata spoke again:
"Those who have not yet trained must not treat this with negligence or contempt; it is not that the meeting of 'this' and 'that' is a matter of excessive toil, for to follow such toil is to err.
If one perceives that 'this' and 'that' are likewise the essentials of the Buddha’s teachings, they are as they ought to be according to the sequence of practice."
If one abandons this toil, observing its beginning and end as the foremost virtue of protection, one will surely abide in correctness and come to know the wisdom that is about to sever this toil.
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘Furthermore, a person must not treat another with contempt; this is not the proper time [for such conduct].
The Tathāgata possesses this knowledge which I do not possess; therefore, one should not respond to others with anger, wrath, or resentment.’”

If one enters the temple, one stands outside the temple gate and bows with the five limbs touching the ground; only then does one withdraw and enter the temple. That [temple] is the abode of emptiness, the abode of compassion, pity, joy, and protection, and the abode of those who dwell correctly in the right sequence. Because they have attained this, it enables me to attain the abode of the temple; it is for them that it is so.
"Because those who distance themselves from official rank and home are the ones who attain the Way.
I have restrained myself through fasting and precepts; such is my self-restraint. This was intended to encourage leaving the home life.

Never before had there been a bodhisattva who attained the Way while remaining at home; they all left the home life and entered the mountains and marshes. They regarded entering the mountains and marshes as the means to attain the Way, thereby disparaging those who dwell at home.

Now, leaving the household life is praised by the wise as being as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; yet, compared to my single day of sacrificial rites, all those acts of giving are surpassed in excellence by the intention of leaving the household life.
Why is this? Because one gives to those who are inferior;
how much more so when giving to those who lack faith, are ungrateful, or are thieves, evildoers, kings, and great ministers?
"It is not that his giving is considered real or sufficient, nor that he possesses the practice of precepts and learning.
Therefore, one who enters a temple should observe what is practiced by the entire assembly of *bhikṣus*: which *bhikṣu* is possessed of great learning?"
What constitutes one who elucidates the sutras?
What constitutes one who upholds the vinaya?
What constitutes one who serves as a messenger?
What is it to be a bodhisattva who upholds the treasury?
What is it to be one who dwells in the mountains and marshes?
What is it to be one who practices receiving offerings?
What is one who practices contemplation?
What is one who practices the Way?
What is a bodhisattva on the path?
Who are the assistants?
Who are the presiding officers?
They are those who observe all that the assembly of mendicants performs.
One should practice according to what is performed, acting in accordance with what one emulates;
one must not harbor mutual jealousy.

If one speaks of the marketplace while in the temple, or speaks of the temple while in the marketplace, one should therefore be careful to guard one's words and conduct. One must not speak of matters from within the temple in the marketplace, nor should one speak of matters from the marketplace within the temple.

"Therefore, serving those who are learned is for the purpose of cultivating and refining one's learning; serving those who clarify the scriptures is for the purpose of resolving doubts regarding the interpretation of the scriptures;
and serving those who uphold the Vinaya is for the purpose of resolving matters concerning the transcendence of calamities and offenses."
To serve and honor the Bodhisattvas who uphold the profound treasury is to clarify the skillful means of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).

If there are those who have removed their impurities (bhikṣus) who lack alms bowls or lack Dharma robes, one should provide and bestow them upon them, ensuring that they do not harbor envy toward others.
Why is this? Because people take jealousy as a fetter; therefore, one should diligently protect ordinary persons who do not conform to proper conduct. Why is this?
Ordinary people are subject to loss, while those who accord with the proper demeanor are free from loss.
If there are those who have removed their defilements but have not yet entered the right path, they may accumulate Dharma robes or accumulate alms bowls.
Therefore, that bhikṣu uses the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to guide them.

Why is this? Because there is a corresponding principle to the matter: one accumulates material things for the sake of attaining the Path; if there are those whose accumulated tranquility of mind is discordant, one should reconcile them.
If the True Dharma is about to decline, one should risk even one's own life to protect and preserve it;
if one sees a mendicant suffering from illness, one should provide blood and flesh so that the patient may be healed.
“Householder!
If a lay bodhisattva does not practice giving, he does not prohibit others from doing so;
if he does give, he never feels regret.”
If there are any roots of manifold virtues, they take this intention as their primary guide.
Householder!
Whether it be these various matters, these various categories, or these various duties, such is the way for a bodhisattva living at home who cultivates the Path.

Furthermore, when the World-Honored One was expounding these teachings and precepts for the practice of householders who are bodhisattvas, there were one thousand people who all resolved their minds to seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
additionally, two thousand gods and humans became free from dust and defilement regarding all dharmas, and the Dharma-eye arose within them.
Thereupon, the householder Śreṣṭhidāraka addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "World-Honored One,
the Tathāgata has extensively expounded upon the grounds of good and evil for the householders who are bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, one should practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, contemplation, and wisdom; these are what should be enacted upon this Great Way.
This, O Blessed One, is the essential point!
Regarding the practices performed by a bodhisattva who has left home to cultivate the Way, I pray that you will manifest even a small portion of them as a virtue.
O Blessed One! How does a bodhisattva who has left home conduct themselves?
"And what is the practice he performs?
The World-Honored One said to the householder Śreṇika:
"Excellent, householder!"
Now you have asked the Tathāgata about the practices of a bodhisattva who has left the household life to cultivate the Way.
Excellent, householder!

I shall explain for you the matters concerning a bodhisattva who has left the household life and their specific practices; you should exert yourself, apply yourself well, and contemplate them with mindfulness.
The householder Ghoṣila accepted the instruction and listened to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said: "Householder!
When a bodhisattva leaves home to cultivate the Way, even if their head were on fire, they would—as if clad in armor—exert themselves with diligence to seek wisdom.
For one who has left home, the beginning is thus; subsequently, they cultivate and refine themselves according to the sacred scriptures.
And what is meant by the sacred scriptures of those who have gone forth from home?
It is said that obtaining a single robe is sufficient, and one should consider this virtuous;
likewise, a single meal, a single bed, and a single medical treatment for illness and weakness are sufficient, and one should consider these virtuous.
This is what constitutes the sacred scriptures (āgama). Why are they called sacred scriptures?
Because they serve to cultivate and refine all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), they are therefore called sacred scriptures.
"Furthermore, for a bodhisattva who has left the household life to cultivate the Way, there are ten virtues of contentment by which they wear the Dharma robes upon their bodies.
What are these ten?
They wear the Dharma robes upon their bodies out of a sense of shame and modesty;..."
One wears the Dharma robes to avoid wind and heat;
one wears the Dharma robes to ward off mosquitoes, gadflies, and horseflies;
and one wears the Dharma robes because one desires to manifest the appearance of one whose mind is stilled.
Furthermore, because this Dharma robe is the deity of the ten directions, one wears the Dharma robe upon the body;
because one suffers from the separation from sensual pleasure, one does not delight in the pleasure of sensuality;
because one finds joy in attaining purity, one eliminates and severs the pleasures of worldly toil.
One does not consider physical plumpness to be the practice of this Way;
rather, one dwells in the heavy responsibility of the Noble Path, and I likewise cultivate myself therein.
It is as if at one time possessing the Dharma-robe, and because of wearing that Dharma-robe.
One should reflect upon these ten virtues until the end of one's life, dwelling in seclusion and tranquility, refraining from begging.
What are the ten?
First, I sustain my life through my own karma alone, and not through any other karma.
If anyone comes to give me alms, I shall first cultivate the Three Jewels and only thereafter accept their gift;
if I wish to beg from others, yet they do not wish to give, it is because I have not extended compassion to them.

I shall eat only the food obtained through my own practice, so as not to violate the instructions of the Tathāgata, to establish the foundation for the heavy responsibility of contentment, to subdue arrogance, and to achieve the root virtue of the invisible crown of the head.
I also observe the practice of giving as if it were my own instruction;

when I go forth to beg for alms, I maintain no partiality toward men or women, regarding all people in the world with an equal mind so that I may fulfill the great responsibility of attaining all-encompassing wisdom.
"It is so, householder!
These ten virtues are that which the renunciant bodhisattva observes within himself until the end of his life: dwelling in seclusion and quietude, he does not practice begging."
If someone comes to invite me to their residence, and that person’s intention is one of faith and joy in the Way, it is not appropriate for me to go there;
even if I were to go for a meal, I may accept the offering only if I can thereby benefit myself and also benefit others.
I teach that a bodhisattva may seek this;
these are the ten virtues by which one may observe oneself and dwell overnight seated beneath a tree.
What are the ten?
He went forth with freedom;
he was not designated as existing;
his bed and bedding were such that he did not close the door.
They dwell in mountains and marshes, having abandoned and distanced themselves from craving;
they cultivate virtue through few desires and few concerns;
and they cast aside their very lives, cherishing nothing for themselves.
One delights in solitude and seclusion, remaining aloof from attachment to social gatherings;
one cultivates the body through ascetic practice and fasting;
and one attains tranquility and single-mindedness through concentration of the mind.
"To contemplate in a secluded place is of no benefit.
It is so, householder!
A bodhisattva who has left the home life should dwell under a tree, observing himself by means of these ten virtues."
"Furthermore, householder!

Should that bodhisattva, having left home to practice the Way and dwell among mountains and marshes, wish to cultivate the sūtras or to recite them with proficiency, he may enter a temple for that purpose."
If one who dwells in a temple directs their intention toward dwelling in mountains and marshes, it is as if they are actually dwelling in those mountains and marshes.
One who practices the seeking of the Dharma conceives of all things as not being "self" and conceives of all dharmas as belonging to others.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva who has left the household life to cultivate the Way wanders among mountains and marshes, they should reflect within themselves: "For what reason do I now wander among these mountains and marshes?
It is not merely by dwelling in mountains and marshes that one is said to have 'stilled the mind'."
Why is this so? Because in this world there are many who do not transform, do not maintain discipline, do not cross over, do not act in accordance with the Way, and do not practice cultivation;

they all roam the mountains and marshes—namely, beasts, various birds, monkeys, apes, and wicked men and thieves—all of whom roam the mountains and marshes, yet they are not called those who have stilled their minds.
As for those who seek to dwell in mountains and marshes as I do, they should do so to fulfill my purpose; their seeking is for the sake of this "stilling of the mind" (*śamatha*).
Furthermore, for what reason does the Bodhisattva still his mind?
That which is called "will" (zhi) means not being disordered, so as to maintain and fully accomplish all affairs;
"hearing" (wen) means having no sense of sufficiency;
and "eloquence" (bianci) means the attainment of refined speech.
One does not diminish great compassion through a heart of loving-kindness;

one does not depart from the five supernormal powers through single-minded devotion, but instead causes the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) to flourish. By repelling all [obstacles] with agility, one practices the wisdom of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) without selective abandonment.

One gathers people together through the gift of Dharma (dharma-dāna), accomplishing the four matters of gathering for the sake of the people, thereby practicing the non-selective abandonment of the six objects of mindfulness.

Through hearing and diligence that are never diminished, one establishes the causal conditions for the path of correctly discerning the beginning and end of phenomena and crossing over; through wisdom that does not enter into worldly matters, one performs the task of protecting the True Dharma.
Taking faith in the retribution of sin and merit as the focus of right view and reflection;

taking the severing of faults as right thought; speaking the Dharma according to what is appropriate as right speech; exhausting all conduct accordingly as right action; and providing for the continuity of the body as right livelihood.
Taking the eradication [of defilements] as right livelihood;
taking the attainment of the Path as right effort;
taking non-forgetfulness and non-negligence as right intention; and taking the attainment of all skillful wisdom as right concentration.
If one takes emptiness as the practice of non-conceptualization;

if one takes detachment from gain as the severance of worldly ties; then one relies on the meaning rather than the letter, relies on the Dharma rather than the person, and relies on wisdom rather than consciousness.

In the exegesis of this text, we do not interpret the meaning according to the concluding sections; rather, this principle is what the masters of logic call the seeker who has left the household life to seek the cessation of the mind.

Furthermore, one who leaves the household life to cultivate the Way should not engage in many worldly affairs. Because one contemplates the root and the branches in this manner, one should not engage in such affairs for the sake of all sentient beings; a person of clear wisdom does not merely refrain from engaging with a single individual.
Furthermore, there are four activities for a renunciant bodhisattva, as taught by the Tathāgata.
What are these four?
The first is: to engage in the activity of expounding the sūtras.
Second, to engage in affairs with those who approach others;
third, to engage in affairs with those who make offerings to the Tathāgata;
fourth, to engage in affairs with those who give rise to all keen intentions without distraction—one should avoid engaging excessively with those who are improper.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva wanders among mountains and marshes, he should examine himself: "For what reason have I come here?
He reflects: "I have come here because of fear."
What is meant by fear?

This assembly fears engaging in lust, anger, delusion, pride, and self-indulgence; it fears evil friends; it fears envy and stinginess; it fears forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures; it fears fame, reputation, honor, and profit; it fears claiming to have seen what was not seen, claimed to have heard what was not heard, claimed to have known what was not known, and claimed to have understood what was not understood; it fears the defilements of the mind; it fears mutual jealousy; it fears falling into the cycle of birth and death, wandering through the five realms of existence; it fears the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm; it fears the aggregates, death, toil, and celestial sons; it fears the evil paths of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; and it fears all such sudden and manifold evil thoughts.
I have come here; it is not fitting for me to remain at home.
If one is amidst a multitude and practices conduct that does not accord with the Way, one cannot escape the fears and anxieties of that assembly.

Furthermore, those former bodhisattvas who were able to escape and transcend the fears of the multitude did so entirely through the power and influence of dwelling in mountain retreats; thus they attained the state of fearlessness, which is called "spontaneity."
Therefore, out of fear, desiring to transcend all fears, I have come to dwell in the mountains and marshes.
Furthermore, all these fears arise from the birth of the body; it is because of attachment to the body that one cultivates the body, and because of this body that one cherishes the body.
It arises from the body of accumulation, the body of volition;
the body of view, the body of station;
the body of perception, and the body of protection.

Even if one dwells in the mountains or marshes because of a mind directed toward the body—cherishing the body, cultivating the body, loving the body, thinking of the body, viewing the body, abiding in the body, conceiving of the body, possessing the body, or protecting the body—then my dwelling in the mountains and marshes is merely empty.
Furthermore, those who dwell in mountains and marshes conceive no notion of a self;
those who dwell in mountains and marshes have no notions of diversity;

those who dwell in mountains and marshes do not engage in doctrinal debate, do not cultivate views regarding their own bodies, and are free from inversion. They possess neither the notion of conditioned existence nor the notion of unconditioned liberation, let alone any notion of weariness.
Those who dwell in the mountains and marshes declare:
"All dharmas are utterly tranquil!
All dharmas are without attachment!"
All pleasures are without attachment!
All perceptions are without craving!
Form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch do not cause conflict or discord!
Do not rely on meditative absorptions!
Keep the mind self-composed and undisturbed!
Be wary of the heavy burdens that follow below!
It is by means of this that the vast and boundless marshes are crossed!
Indeed, the scriptures of the Sage are for the purpose of creation!
May all those belonging to the class of the wicked and evil find complete satisfaction!
How great is the burden of having few desires!
How wise is contentment!
Be one who is truly content!
How truly contented!
How truly one who bears the heavy burden with few desires!
How truly worthy!
The practices of the root and the branches have been understood!
The tasks cultivated for the sake of severing all prisons have been completed!
They are thereby rendered eternally resolved and liberated.
“Householder!
It is as if, in the mountains and marshes, there are trees, grasses, and weeds, none of which are to be feared and none of which are to be dreaded.
In this same way, householder!”

When a bodhisattva wanders among mountains and marshes, they should maintain their resolve like the metaphors of grass, trees, walls, and stones; with the body practicing what they have received, who is there to fear?

Through contemplation born of fear, he reflects on the beginning and end of the body: "I have no self at all; I am not a person, not a life-principle, not a man, not a being, not a woman, not prior, not having a prior, not a creator, not one who causes creation, not a giver, and not one who brings about arising."
All these fears arise solely from the perception of non-attainment;
now, I should not create the perception of non-attainment that gives rise to such fear!

Now, I should not give rise to thoughts of failure; rather, I should regard myself as being like trees, grasses, and weeds, likewise silent and without sound, thereby understanding all those dharmas and practicing them fully.
One dwells in mountain and marsh retreats where echoes have ceased, remaining far removed from the dust of lust.
Dwelling in mountain and marsh retreats where there are no echoes means that one is neither "I" nor a possessor of things.

Furthermore, those who roam in the mountains and marshes do so with repeated reflection; they dwell in the mountains and marshes as those who have attained mastery over the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*).
Those who dwell in mountains and marshes harmonize and gather the twelve essences;
those who dwell in mountains and marshes understand all truths;

those who dwell in mountains and marshes know the aggregates (*skandhas*), using smoothness to restrain the emotions and using birds to capture those who enter [the path], never forgetting the intent of the Way.
Praised by all Buddhas and extolled by the multitude of sages, it is that which those wishing to deliver the world attend to.
For those dwelling in mountains and marshes, it is the skillful means for understanding all things with keen wisdom.
Furthermore, as for those who roam among mountains and marshes, they shall before long fulfill the practice of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
How is it that they attain this?
If those who roam among mountains and marshes do not cherish their own bodies or lives, this constitutes the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
If, by virtue of relying on vigor, one accomplishes the three types of carefulness, this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā);
if the mind is not distracted and is likewise entirely alert without deviating from the Way, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā);
as for reaching the point where one does not give rise to [distraction] until the end of one's life, this is the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
If one attains single-mindedness not through diligent exertion, but solely by exalting the root of virtue, this is the perfection of single-mindedness (ekāgratā-pāramitā).

If one perceives all things as being like mountains, marshes, and roads, and thus distinguishes among various phenomena, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā); it is through the Way that the bodhisattva attains these.
"Furthermore, householder!
There are four dharmas that one must cultivate; it is for these that I instruct bodhisattvas to dwell in mountain forests and marshes.
What are the four? "

There may be bodhisattvas who are widely learned and clear in their discernment of the Dharma; if they practice what they have heard regarding the fundamental and derivative aspects of the Dharma, they may dwell in mountains and marshes.

Furthermore, there may be bodhisattvas who have attained the five supernormal powers and wish to bring celestial beings, nāgas, and spirits to spiritual maturity; they may dwell in mountains and marshes.
Or there may be bodhisattvas whose weariness is great; because they find that by not engaging in worldly toil, such weariness becomes diminished, they may dwell in mountains and marshes.
Furthermore, wishing to restrain weariness and encourage themselves, they all rely upon hearing [the Dharma].

Those who travel there obtain the fulfillment of all pure dharmas; only thereafter do they descend to villages, market towns, districts, counties, states, and capitals, where they preach and transmit the Dharma for the sake of the multitude and cultivate the Dharma.
It is thus, Householder! This is my teaching for bodhisattvas dwelling in mountains and marshes.

Furthermore, those who have left the household life to cultivate the Way and roam in mountains and marshes may enter among the multitude for the sake of cultivating and reciting the sutras; yet even when so engaged, they must maintain reverence and remain humble.
Regarding teachers and friends who provide instruction, those who are like lost youths among them should treat them with reverence and not be indolent;
yet regarding one's own practice, one should not neglect the practice of others, nor should one seek to serve or pay homage to them for that reason.
If one were to regard this as observing the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—one who is honored by the Brahmās, Śakras, devas, and all sentient beings;

who is the field of merit for those above and below in heaven and earth; and who does not even seek to be served by others, performing his own tasks without wishing to trouble anyone—how much more so should it be for others?
Having not yet studied, or being only just beginning to study, how can one instead desire others to serve them!
Furthermore, while I am one who should provide for all people in the world, I shall instead provide offerings to others; I do not seek offerings from others at all.
Why is this? O Householder!
Because those who are to be supported cannot receive the assistance of the Dharma for their offerings; thus, my assistance to them is not by means of the Dharma.
Now, those who wish to assist others by means of the Dharma act in this manner:

because they provide such offerings, they consider themselves to be assisting me, yet it is not for the sake of the Dharma. Driven by their own personal attachment to their correct faith, they believe that there is an offering; thus, they become entangled with worldly things and are not those who bring great benefit to others.
Therefore, if you wish to go and visit the Buddha, teachers, or friends, you must first ensure that your physical and mental conduct is resolute; only then may you go with longing.

In my teaching, teachers and friends do not err through unconventional behavior; rather, they accumulate the essence of instruction by not rebuking, but instead by questioning, exhorting, and encouraging the practice of recitation.

Therefore, one who wishes to inspire others through the sutras does not do so for the sake of sacrificing their own life; rather, they cherish and delight in the Dharma, follow the teacher’s intent, and seek the benefit of the Dharma, not seeking the benefits of all forms of honor or reputation.
If one receives even a few lines of a four-line verse from a teacher and recites them;

or if one makes offerings to that teacher through the practice of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom—then even if one were to offer such worship for as many eons as there are syllables in those four-line verses, it would still not constitute the ultimate respect for the teacher. Furthermore, if one offers all conduct characterized by sincerity, honesty, lack of artifice, and freedom from flattery, how could this alone be called "respect for the Dharma"?
"Furthermore, householder!
If such thoughts arise—thoughts endowed with virtue, thoughts regarding the Buddha and also the Dharma, thoughts of self-reproach for one's departure from lust, and thoughts of tranquility."

If one were to cultivate and practice according to these four-line verses for as many eons as there are in their number, even such service rendered to one's teacher would still not constitute the ultimate respect for the Dharma.
Householder!
You should understand this matter:
if it is thus, the merit of the Dharma is incalculable, and the wisdom attained is likewise immeasurable.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva wishes to select the supreme Dharma, they regard even the immeasurable as the veneration of the True Dharma.
Whether it be that contemplation or this hearing of the matters of pure precepts, [it is so].
What are the matters of pure precepts?
For a renunciant bodhisattva, there are four matters of pure precepts.
The first is: composing the scriptures of the noble ones.
Second is to aspire to and delight in the virtue of diligence;
third is not to engage in the affairs of those who dwell at home with those who have left the home life;
fourth is not to flatter those who dwell in mountains or marshes.
These are the four matters of pure precepts for a bodhisattva who has left the household life.
Furthermore, there are four other matters of pure precepts.
What are these four?
By guarding with circumspection the body, the body is free from hindrance;
by guarding with circumspection speech, speech is free from hindrance;
by guarding with circumspection the mind, the mind is free from hindrance.
To depart from and abandon wrong doubts, thereby creating all-encompassing agility of mind—
this is the fourth matter of pure precepts for a bodhisattva who has left the household life.
Furthermore, there are four other matters of pure precepts.
What are the four?
First, knowing through self-awareness;
second, not being conceited.
Third, not to judge others by their physical appearance;
fourth, not to slander or disparage others.
These are the four matters of pure precepts for a bodhisattva who has left the household life.
Furthermore, there are four matters of pure precepts.
What are the four?
First, regarding the aggregates, one has already realized that they are illusory phenomena.
Second, to regard all feelings as the feeling for the Dharma;
third, to regard all sense bases (*āyatana*) as empty aggregates;
fourth, not to follow the conventional rituals of worldly customs.
These are the four matters of pure precepts for a householder who has left the household life as a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are four other matters of pure precepts.
What are the four?
First, not reckoning oneself as a self;
second, distancing oneself from the notion of "this is mine";
third, severing and eliminating the persistence of permanence.
The fourth is the teaching on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
These are the four matters of pure precepts for a bodhisattva who has gone forth from home.
Furthermore, there are another four matters of pure precepts.
What are the four?
First, understanding emptiness;
second, not being afraid of the absence of mental formations.
Third, to regard all people with great compassion;
fourth, to consider the body as something that may be treated with indifference.
These are the four matters of pure precepts for a bodhisattva who has left the household life.
Because he constantly hears of and practices pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*), he contemplates in this manner. What is meant by this pure concentration?

It is that which penetrates all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) without the mental activity being directed toward other matters; it is the resolute mind, the one-pointed mind, the unerring mind, the non-abiding mind, the non-wandering mind, and the mind that dwells within itself. It is the mind that does not engage with sensual desires and contemplates phenomena as illusory: "I am like an illusion, and my passions are likewise. Because there is no further activity, there is nothing that can persist. Having thus trodden the path of correctness, this is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
If a phenomenon exists in accordance with reality, and if this is also called "certainty," one contemplates it as such.
That person constantly hears of pure wisdom. What is this wisdom?
The discerning wisdom regarding all phenomena is what is called "insight" (prajñā).

It is the characteristic of non-appropriation, which is the practice of signlessness; it is the characteristic of non-creation, in which there is no persistence; it is the characteristic of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), in which there is no wandering.
"Therefore, one should manage the household!
To observe the Dharma in this manner is called the practice performed by a renunciant bodhisattva.
Furthermore, while this sutra was being preached, five hundred people conceived the aspiration for supreme, right, and true enlightenment.
Furthermore, the householder Śreṣṭhin and his peers raised their voices together and said:
"It is unprecedented! How marvelous, O Blessed One!
That the well-spoken words of the Tathāgata should be such as this!"
It is the heavy burden of evil conduct that remains within the household;
it is the departure from the household that brings forth all virtues and goodness.
Venerable Saṅgharakṣita!

Having already clarified that householders possess many evil qualities, whereas those who have left the home life possess immeasurable virtues and goodness, would it not be possible for one to follow the World-Honored One, receive the precepts of leaving the home life, and undertake the practice of the seeker (śrāmaṇya)?

The World-Honored One replied, "For one who has left the household life, it is difficult to manage the affairs of a householder; one must be able to thoroughly cultivate pure virtue and skillfully uphold the teachings.
The householder spoke again to the Buddha:
“O World-Honored One!
Although leaving the household life is difficult to undertake, the Tathāgata should nevertheless permit those like us to leave home for the sake of the Way.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One commanded the Bodhisattva Maitreya and the Bodhisattva Sarvācāraśuddha to listen, and he raised up those householders and others.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya brought forth two hundred householders, and the Bodhisattva Sarvācāraśuddha brought forth three hundred householders, who left their homes to practice the Way.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the householder Viśākha:
"What have you seen, that while living in the kingdom and residing at home, you are able to delight in the noble path of leaving home for the sake of the Dharma?"
The householder Śreṇika replied to Ānanda:
"It is not because I covet bodily pleasure or desire to bring about the happiness of sentient beings that I dwell as a householder!"
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata is one who has personally realized the self; he dwells at home with that which he has received made firm.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!"
“Have you already seen the householder Śreṇika?
“So it is, Blessed One!
I have seen the householder Śreṇika.”

“Ānanda! Within this Bhadrakalpa, those who have achieved such accomplishment through renouncing the household life exceed even those from a hundred kalpas; they are not matched by those of the past.”
Why is this so? Ānanda!
Furthermore, among a thousand bodhisattvas who have left the household life to practice the Way, there may not be one with such virtue as this householder possesses.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One!
What should this Dharma discourse be named?"
"And how should it also be upheld?
The World-Honored One said: "Therefore, Ānanda!"
This sutra-dharma is titled "The Transformation of the Householder and the Renunciant";
uphold it. It is also titled "The Transformation of Inner Nature and Virtue";
uphold it. It is also titled "The Profound Inquiry"; uphold it.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those who hear this Dharma of the sutra will possess a supreme and powerful diligence that fulfills the Dharma;
their practice of the path through diligent effort in all modes of conduct cannot compare with this.
Therefore, Ānanda!

If you wish to arouse diligence, if you wish to encourage others, if you wish to establish a single merit, or if you wish to bring about the virtues of the multitude of people, you must hear, receive, and practice this Dharma of the sutra.
I entrust this Dharma discourse to you, Ānanda, so that it may be circulated among the multitude.
Why is this? Because it is the correct practice of all virtuous dharmas.
"Ānanda! This Dharma of the sutra is precisely the correct principle.

When the World-Honored One had spoken thus, Ānanda rejoiced; as did the householder Śrigupta, the devas, and humans, as well as King Prasenajit. Once the World-Honored One had finished speaking, they all entered into reflection.
Postscript to the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra* The postscript states:
Now, if one does not look into a bright mirror, one will not see one's own form; if one does not praise the sacred scriptures, one will not see one's own true nature.
Emotions may be true or false; natures may be soft or firm; aspirations may be pure or fierce; intentions may be obscure or clear; and cognitions may be shallow or deep—they cannot all be the same.

Without beholding the sacred scriptures, there is no means by which one may achieve self-illumination; for this reason, the Buddha composed this sutra, titled *The Mirror of the Dharma*, and bestowed it upon us.

May the supreme bodhisattvas transmit its teachings throughout the world, so that those of discernment and virtue, scholars who attain thorough understanding, and practitioners whose resolve is upright, may swiftly realize unsurpassed holiness.

Lady Kang possessed the virtue of grain and was broad-minded, erudite, and quick-witted; she composed commentaries and expounded upon the principles of the teachings. How much more so, then, for this scripture, which is so luminous and was composed by the Divine and the Sage?

Among the multitude of sages and immortals in the heavens above and the world below, there are none who do not bow their heads in reverence, receiving [his teachings] as a luminous model. Through them, scholars increase their wisdom and practitioners attain deliverance; such instances are beyond counting.

Yet in these degenerate times, those who have only recently begun their studies possess neither broad vision nor extensive learning; they instead rely on their own private biases to disparage the authentic teachings and contravene the scriptures—is this not truly lamentable!
To claim to study Buddhism while contravening the Buddha’s teachings—what could one possibly seek from such a path?

Long ago, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a person who inverted a single character of the Buddha’s name; subsequently, he incurred the retribution of being blind for five hundred lifetimes, remaining in a state of blinding darkness for a very long duration.
Upon reaching the time of Śākyamuni Buddha,
that person, having heard of the Buddha’s holy virtue, came from afar to take refuge and was thus able to obtain salvation.
The Buddha saw him from afar and called out to him!
His eyes opened immediately; he threw himself down in repentance, begging for his illness to be cured.
The Buddha said, "Your transgression is now finished!
There shall be no further blame from this point on. Behold, one must not fail to be cautious!"
"If a person can again bring their mind back to repentance, reforming the past and cultivating the future, this is also the intention of the worthy!
[This is] the Postscript to the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra*."
